essay_title: Bearing Up in The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African
special_features: Continuous prose with three internal sub-section titles ('Time Doesn't Add Up', 'Attachments / Feeling', 'Bearing Up')
Operates on Equiano's 1789 Interesting Narrative as primary text — Penguin Classics ed. Vincent Carretta 2003

outline_prose.prose: Gross opens the chapter with two yoked epigraphs — Equiano's 1789 declaration that, after three or four years in England, he had become 'inured' to ship-service, considered himself 'happily situated,' and was 'almost an Englishman' (Narrative 77); and Merleau-Ponty's 1945 figure of the 'intentional arc' which projects 'roundabout as our past, our future, our human setting,' unifies sense and motility, and which 'goes limp' in illness (Phenomenology of Perception 136). The pairing is programmatic: Equiano's apparent rhetoric of adjustment looks like a perfect proof-text for situated cognition's main thesis until one notices the Merleau-Pontian arc has illness built into it. Gross flags slavery-as-inconvenience as an absurd understatement and announces a tripartite plan — time, attachment/feeling, bearing up — in each of which Equiano will appear to support the science of happiness and the theory of situated cognition, only to dissipate that support into queries and counter-arguments. The chapter's working register is 'local problematic at the intersection of science and the humanities,' with both directions of traffic preserved: situated-cognition is enriched by literary rhetorical analysis, and the humanities receive from Kahneman et al. a methodological sensitivity to anchoring effects.

The 'Time Doesn't Add Up' section opens with the slave ship as the first object that 'salutes' the young Equiano's eyes upon his arrival at the African coast, an object that resets his calendar to year zero (Narrative 55-60). Gross reads the Middle Passage scene paraphrastically — heat, perspiration, smells, chains, groans, the conditions both 'insupportable' (for living) and 'inconceivable' (for knowing) — without ever quoting at length, citing instead by page. The 'so many sheep in the fold' figure that captures the live cargo on landing at Barbados (60) becomes a hinge: year zero foreshadows seconds — second nature, second coming. Equiano is a predestinarian (Narrative 119) before any Methodist exposure, and the Igbo Creator (40) is already, for Gross, the same God 'who in very deed leads the blind' (63), who arrives 'overrated' as creature-comfort. Gross summarizes four temporalities at work in the Narrative: ontogenic, historical, prophetic, and prevenient-grace, the fourth cutting through the other three.

Gross then engages the double-consciousness reading of 'almost an Englishman' (Carretta, Henry Louis Gates Jr.) and refuses it: he does not want a sense that splits in two if that means each perspective can be measured against the other via some common denominator. Du Bois (Souls 1903) is registered as a critique of Kantian unity of experience; Fanon's 'Lived Experience of the Black Man' (1952) yields the formula 'the situation is unbearable' that Gross will recover in the final section. Iris Marion Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl' (1980, On Female Body Experience 2005) and Gayle Salamon's Assuming a Body (2010) extend the critique: sense-data are not neutral; the rubber-hand experiment, dysphoric circuits through hostile gaze, and patriarchy-restricted embodied space all locate sensation in the social. Fred Moten's 'Knowledge of Freedom' (CR 2004) presses past double-consciousness toward 'knowledge that moves from somewhere on the other side of either reason or experience.' Equiano's gratitude to Pascal — who sells him just when freedom appears within reach (Narrative 93-94) — is irreducibly ironic. The opening passage is a 'thanks a lot.'

Gross then mounts the chapter's longest engagement with hedonic psychology. Kahneman and Miller's 'Norm Theory' (1986) supplies emotional amplification and the availability of counterfactuals; Brickman, Janoff-Bulman & Coates (1978) supply the hedonic treadmill (lottery winners, paraplegics); Kahneman's distinction between becoming-paraplegic and being-paraplegic (1999, p.16) gestures at the analytic difficulty. Gross extracts from Kahneman a triadic disciplinary map: experimental sciences focus on the 'predictably irrational,' social sciences on the 'practically irrational,' humanities on the 'possibly irrational.' He then turns to Norbert Schwarz and Fritz Strack's chapter in the same Well-Being volume, whose taxonomy of complicating factors in subjective-well-being reports (question-order, conversational norms, episodic chunking, counterfactual availability, direction of comparison, social-improvement expectations, peer-comparison, attention-manipulation, self-censoring) Gross reads as 'a veritable taxonomy of social experiment rhetoric.' The methodological punt — wait for cognitive science to clarify — Gross rejects: the rhetorical insights are already legitimating. Equiano's 'Was Equiano really happy?' is decomposed through layered grammatical retrospection ('he wrote that he considered himself happily situated'), arriving at the eighteenth-century gloss of 'happy' as 'by chance' (OED, n.22).

Gross now executes the chapter's most distinctive rhetorical move: a line-by-line interleaving of Alva Noe's Out of Our Heads (p.51) with Equiano's biography. Noe's claim that maturation is growth into one's environmental situation is glossed with Equiano considering himself happily situated; Noe's 'we grow apart but attach to the world without' is glossed with 'Equiano is almost an Englishman'; the locking-in figure (a dance) is replaced with the literal lock-in of slavery. The move performs Gross's thesis: pragmatic phenomenology's friendliness with environment can absorb Equiano's case only by suppressing the hostility coefficient of his particular environment. Time-as-felt-slowdown is then read into the Middle Passage astonishment ('attonare: to strike with a thunderbolt').

The 'Attachments / Feeling' section opens with Noe's baby-caretaker dyad and the rubber-hand experiment, both of which dissolve nerve-attachment into a relational attachment of 'common fate.' Equiano's coordination with Pascal exemplifies this — but, Gross insists, would the interest of the slave finally be identified with that of his master? Gross retrieves Carretta's biographical formulation (Equiano, the African 2005, p.98 and p.122) of 'vested interest': the overseer lacks the owner's vested interest in slave well-being, and the freed Equiano discovers that no one in a race-based-slavery environment has a vested interest in his well-being — a 'terrible irony' that makes him in some ways more secure as a slave. Gross then locates the chapter's pivotal philosophical move: Merleau-Ponty's late 'Freedom' chapter, particularly the line 'It may even happen when I am in danger that my human situation abolishes my biological one, that my body lends itself without reserve to action' (Phenomenology of Perception 84). This is the Hegelian strand that pragmatic phenomenology — Hubert Dreyfus is named as exemplar — loses. The slave is perpetually endangered; the free black is endangered too. 'Black freedom in this legal sense dissipates into the white world.'

Gross then offers a sustained exegesis of Hegel's master-slave dialectic (Phenomenology of Spirit ¶¶186-193 in the Findlay translation, accessed via Hegel-by-Hypertext). The bondsman's Anerkennung is foreclosed not just ideologically but materially. Findlay's gloss is quoted: 'the bondsman acquiesces in the situation, and becomes in fact part and parcel of the total objective situation.' Hegel's conclusion at ¶193 — 'The truth of the independent consciousness is accordingly the consciousness of the bondsman' — anchors the rest of the chapter. Crucially this Hegelian unbalanced relationship does not tend toward homeostasis; there is no living-wage or equality-before-the-law threshold that would 'right' the mutation. Equiano grapples with precisely this impossibility. The Hegelian mutation lives on around an incomplete negation: complete destruction of the other would be complete destruction of the self. Neither stoicism nor skepticism nor 'unhappy consciousness' resolve it (¶¶198, 206, 217). Merleau-Ponty's extraordinary three-page footnote at 172n1 — comparing general strike to sickness, both forcing decisive factors into visibility — is Gross's evidence that Merleau-Ponty, properly read in the Marxist line, retains the resources to think the social-body going limp.

Gross then characterizes Equiano's happy situation as positing an attitude toward (subjection-as-no-longer-terror, master-as-gratitude-object, English-as-social-identity) rather than describing a first-person state. 'Rhetorical' here means two things: (a) effective — the passage operates on the reader irrespective of authorial intention (the intentional fallacy hazard, citing Wimsatt & Beardsley 1946); the irony is figured by inhabiting convention; (b) positing-a-social-relationship — pathos in the classical lexicon, requiring an audience to appear as such. Samuel Johnson's Rambler 60 (1750) on identification through recognition is invoked to demonstrate that Equiano's abolitionist effect does not require sincere happiness or misery; identification can be the modest adoption of a proposal, or the appeal to the eyes of God.

The 'Bearing Up' section opens with the question of givenness. For Noe, what is given depends on the relations we bear (Out of Our Heads 83). Sara Ahmed (Queer Phenomenology 2006) is recruited as methodological ally: objects gather along certain lines; heterosexuality is registered phenomenologically; orientation depends on taking certain points of view as given. Gross then proposes a methodological principle: narrative literature reveals what is given by tracking what its character senses — 'books are orientation devices.' The Interesting Narrative is abolitionist by offering the orientation that makes abolition necessary. The next paragraph paraphrases Equiano's sale to Captain Doran (Narrative 97): the wished-for land lost, the cursed tide, the call upon death to relieve horrors. Gross spotlights the alliteration born/bore as exploiting morphology, then mounts an OED 'bear' excursus (verb senses I–IV: carry, sustain, thrust, bring forth; 21 'bear up' as Burke's 'Bearing up against those vicissitudes of fortune' 1796; nautical sense 37; noun senses including 'deportment' Much Ado 1600 and Pope's 'Bearings and Ties' 1733).

Two dynamics emerge. First, the practical: name-bearing. Pascal forces 'Gustavus Vassa' on Equiano over his preferred 'Jacob,' beating him until he submits (Narrative 64). Equiano is excluded from the systems of knowledge that would render his identity intelligible — and, Gross notes, 'not ever' admitted, as Afro-Pessimism argues. The Robert King certificate (Montserrat, January 26, 1767) is reproduced verbatim from Narrative 163-164: it bears Equiano's slave-name and certifies his 'behaviour while in his service' — flimsy attachment, yet worth gold. The natality-sustainability dynamic is also practical: the tide bears Equiano as the broken Pascal-promise unfolds. Following Ahmed's analysis of direction-following as social investment promising return (Queer Phenomenology 17), Gross amends Ahmed: Equiano is pressed into service outside consent or social contract, so the very recognition-of-living-a-certain-way is false-witness. He was ready to curse the tide, ready to curse God, ready to curse his own birth — but, in retrospective qualification, he did not. He carried what he was ready to abandon. 'One might even say his suffering at this point shows Equiano bearing the cross for Jesus in a manner he could barely recognize at the time.'

The chapter closes on the conversion-at-sea episode (Cadiz voyage, March 1775, Narrative 198-199): ship strikes rock, Equiano cannot swim, feels no dread, and the Toplady hymn comes to mind (Augustus Montague Toplady, Psalms and Hymns 1776, No. 312 'The Spiritual Victory,' identified via Carretta n.43): 'Christ is my pilot wise, my compass is his word... How can I sink with such a prop, / That bears the world and all things up?' Gross then reproduces the long Mount Calvary 'unsealing' set-piece (Narrative 189-190) with his own annotation and underscoring of what Merleau-Ponty would call the intentional arc rehabilitated. The scriptures become an 'unsealed book'; Equiano sees the crucified Saviour at Mount Calvary; Romans 7:9-25, John 3:5 ('born again'), Romans 8:14 ('the Spirit you received does not make you slaves'), Acts 8:26 ('the Ethiopian was willing to be saved') are densely keyed. Mary Wollstonecraft's Analytical Review (1789, vol. 4, pp. 27-29) panned this latter material as 'rather tiresome' — Gross rejects the verdict. The standard four-step conversion allegory (godly sadness, rebirth, challenge, manifestation) is conceded as conventional, but the key analytic point is that Equiano's senses are unified only at the price of having been incapable of self-bearing. Comfortable conversation with the world is not available to him. A litany of the inoperable follows (Narrative 109, 110, 111, 112, 161-162): enslavement of one's own progeny; buried virtue; violated natural rights; no common currency for rational communication; the West-Indies inadmissibility of black testimony — which leaves Equiano without recourse when Robert King defaults on a debt. As a slave, Equiano bears down on a world that is not his own; then Jesus bears everything. He ends 'neither here nor there.'

concepts.label: bearing up
concepts.definition: Equiano's titular emotional-rhetorical disposition: a way of carrying / sustaining / enduring (OED 'bear' senses I–II + 21 'bear up') under conditions in which the bearer is excluded from the social-recognitional structures that would normally make endurance intelligible. Not stoic endurance, not pragmatic adjustment, not the Hegelian bondsman's 'acquiescence' alone — but a rhetorical structure of carrying-what-one-was-ready-to-curse, with the carrying borne, at the limit, by Christ as the 'prop that bears the world and all things up.'

concepts.label: happily situated
concepts.definition: Equiano's loaded phrase from Narrative 77 (the chapter's first epigraph). Gross reads it as a rhetorical posture that posits a relational attitude (toward subjection, master, English identity) rather than describing a first-person hedonic state. The eighteenth-century OED gloss of 'happy' as 'by chance' (n.22) underwrites a deeper ironization.

concepts.label: vested interests
concepts.definition: Carretta's biographical formulation (Equiano, the African 2005, pp. 98 and 122) re-deployed by Gross as analytic: the owner has a vested interest in slave well-being; the overseer does not; and a freed black in a race-based-slavery environment finds no one with a vested interest in his well-being. The formula makes Equiano paradoxically more secure as a slave. Interests can be vested differently from feelings: Equiano may feel attached to the very relationships that subject him.

concepts.label: attachment + time
concepts.definition: Gross's analytic pair: feeling-attachment is always temporally indexed (gratitude requires duration), and time is measured through attachment ('my master treated me always extremely well'). The hedonic treadmill is the scientific name for one slice of this pair; the Hegelian master-slave dialectic is the philosophical name for another.

concepts.label: black freedom dissipates
concepts.definition: Gross's diagnosis that in a race-based-slavery environment, legal manumission of a black person dissipates into the white world. A free black is constantly threatened by the institutions that already define environment as hostile (kidnap, resale, unrecoverable debts, inadmissibility of testimony). The legal piece of paper attesting equality cannot make life bearable.

concepts.label: race-based slavery as environment
concepts.definition: Slavery treated not as an institution that acts upon individuals from outside but as the environment within which sense-perception, attachment, and bearing take their shape. This positions the chapter to feed into Gross's broader Gibson-affordance project (Ch. 3) while distinguishing this environment as one of negative / hostile affordance specifically.

concepts.label: spiritual autobiography
concepts.definition: Genre frame for Equiano's conversion narrative (Mount Calvary 'unsealing,' Narrative 189-190). Gross concedes conventionality of the four-step allegorical structure (godly sadness → rebirth → challenge → manifestation of new creature) while insisting the form's 'giving' of senses to Equiano executes the chapter's analytic, not merely confessional, work.

concepts.label: intentional arc
concepts.definition: Merleau-Pontian figure (Phenomenology of Perception 136, second epigraph) for the projecting structure that unifies past/future/setting/situation and the senses. Gross's reading is double: the arc gives Noe and the situated-cognitive theorists their license, and its 'going limp' in illness gives Gross his lever for reading social pathology (general strike, slavery) as analogous to bodily illness.

concepts.label: Hegelian strand in Merleau-Ponty
concepts.definition: Gross's chapter-central interpretive claim: Merleau-Ponty's 'Freedom' chapter (Phenomenology of Perception 84, Smith trans.) contains a Hegelian-Marxist line in which the human situation can 'abolish the biological one' — a line Hubert Dreyfus's pragmatic-phenomenological reading systematically loses.

concepts.label: prevenient-grace temporality
concepts.definition: The fourth of Gross's four temporalities of the Narrative (alongside ontogenic, historical, and prophetic). It cuts through the other three. It is what makes Equiano's narrative 'interesting' rather than merely picaresque, and it makes a place for the untimely (the unhurt fall from ship's ballast, instances 'which might not otherwise have found a place here').

concepts.label: double consciousness as insufficient
concepts.definition: Gross registers Du Bois's Souls of Black Folks (1903) doubling and Fanon's 1952 'lived experience of the black man,' but refuses any reading in which the two perspectives can be measured by a common denominator. Moten's 'Knowledge of Freedom' is positioned beyond doubling.

concepts.label: rhetorical = effective + positing-a-social-relationship
concepts.definition: Gross's two-pronged gloss of 'rhetorical' in this chapter: (a) effective — operates on the reader irrespective of (and at the risk of) authorial intention (Wimsatt & Beardsley intentional-fallacy hazard); (b) positing a social relationship — pathos in the classical sense, requiring an audience to appear as such.

concepts.label: possibly / practically / predictably irrational
concepts.definition: Gross's disciplinary triad: experimental sciences interested in the predictably irrational, social sciences in the practically irrational, humanities in the possibly irrational — the last being how emotions figure the world around limit-cases that qualify common sense.

concepts.label: hedonic treadmill
concepts.definition: Brickman, Janoff-Bulman & Coates (1978) and Brickman & Campbell (1971) thesis that improving circumstances yield diminishing returns. Gross uses lottery-winner and paraplegic case studies. The becoming-paraplegic / being-paraplegic distinction (Kahneman 16) is the analytic refinement.

concepts.label: Norm Theory + emotional amplification
concepts.definition: Kahneman & Miller (1986) thesis that affective response to an event is enhanced relative to a counterfactual norm. Gross applies it to Equiano: as years pass, the counterfactual ('what might have been' — return to Africa) dissipates, and so does the amplitude of terror.

concepts.label: rhetoric of experience (Noe)
concepts.definition: Alva Noe's claim in Varieties of Presence (Harvard 2012) that perception is not sensation but 'an activity of securing access to the world by cultivating the right critical stance,' and that human experience has a 'rhetorical structure.' Gross seizes this as the situated-cognition theorist's spontaneous admission that the humanities are already inside cognitive science.

concepts.label: orientation / objects-gathering (Ahmed)
concepts.definition: Sara Ahmed's Queer Phenomenology (Duke 2006) figure for how objects gather along certain lines not others, how heterosexuality phenomenologically registers as given, and how 'discomfort... allows things to move.' Gross uses Ahmed as methodological ally throughout the bearing-up section, then 'amends' her by noting that Equiano is pressed into service outside the social-investment frame Ahmed presupposes.

concepts.label: books as orientation devices
concepts.definition: Gross's methodological principle: narrative literature reveals what is given to a character by tracking what the character senses. 'Some books are largely about just this orientation process' — Interesting Narrative makes abolition necessary by offering the orientation that makes abolition makes-sense.

concepts.label: bear / born / bore (OED morphological cluster)
concepts.definition: The OED-grounded morphological cluster Equiano's prose exploits: I. carry; II. sustain; III. thrust, press; IV. bring forth; + 'bear up' (21); + nautical 37. Gross argues Equiano's alliteration is not stylistic ornament but a deep working of the language to figure his condition.

concepts.label: name-bearing (Gustavus Vassa imposition)
concepts.definition: Pascal forces 'Gustavus Vassa' on Equiano in place of Equiano's preferred 'Jacob' (Narrative 64). The forced name-bearing is the practical instantiation of the larger problem of bearing identity in a system of knowledge from which one is constitutively excluded.

concepts.label: certificate of behavior (Robert King)
concepts.definition: The Montserrat, January 26, 1767, document signed by Robert King and reproduced verbatim in Narrative 163-164: 'The bearer hereof, Gustavus Vassa, was my slave for upwards of three years, during which he has always behaved himself well.' Bears Equiano's slave-name; is the flimsiest attachment yet worth gold.

concepts.label: litany of the inoperable
concepts.definition: The closing inventory at PDF 86: a world where a master enslaves his own progeny (Narrative 109), where 'every principle and all sentiments of virtue' are buried (110), where natural rights are violated (111), where no common currency for rational communication exists (112), and where black testimony is inadmissible (161-162 — Robert King defaulting on a debt).

concepts.label: Afro-Pessimism (engaged but not endorsed)
concepts.definition: Gross's reference (n.42) to Jared Sexton's 'The Social Life of Social Death: On Afro-Pessimism and Black Optimism' (InTensions 2011); also Frank Wilderson, Fred Moten. Used in the chapter to underwrite the claim that Equiano was excluded — 'not ever' — from systems of knowledge that make identity intelligible. Gross stops short of endorsing the program wholesale.

concepts.label: comfort (eighteenth-century sense)
concepts.definition: OED-tracked eighteenth-century semantics in which 'comfort' is first what God can give you; 'creature-comfort' arrives overrated (B. Wallin, Eternal Mansion 1769). The chapter exploits this lexical pre-history to ironize the modern hedonic-psychology vocabulary.

concepts.label: going limp (Merleau-Ponty)
concepts.definition: Merleau-Ponty's figure for the failure of the intentional arc in illness. Gross extends it via Merleau-Ponty's three-page footnote at 172n1 to the social body: a general strike makes factors of production visible the way illness makes vital rhythm visible. The slave's situation is the social body going limp.

concepts.label: Anerkennung foreclosed
concepts.definition: Hegelian recognition foreclosed not just ideologically but materially — the structure of master-slave at Phenomenology of Spirit ¶¶186-193. Gross uses Findlay's commentary via Hegel-by-Hypertext.

concepts.label: unsealed book
concepts.definition: Equiano's figure for the moment of scriptural revelation at Mount Calvary (Narrative 189-190). Gross underscores it as the conversion-scene's central rhetorical gesture and ties it back to the Du Boisian veil metaphor.

concepts.label: intentional fallacy hazard
concepts.definition: Wimsatt & Beardsley's 1946 stricture, invoked by Gross at n.37, to qualify any reading of Equiano's effects as if reducible to authorial intention. The rhetorical force operates by inhabiting convention, with the irony figured at the level of the convention itself.

concepts.label: prosthetic emotion (Equiano application)
concepts.definition: The Intro-level concept of prosthetic emotion (Imitation of Christ as performative emotion-installation) gets its first major in-text demonstration in this chapter: Equiano's bearing-the-cross-for-Jesus is precisely a prosthesis that completes a rhetorical-emotional disposition the slave could not muster on his own.

positions.stance: 'Bearing up' names a rhetorical-emotional disposition that exceeds both submission and resistance, and that exceeds pragmatic-phenomenology's vocabulary of comfortable habituation.
positions.opposition: Pragmatic phenomenology (Dreyfus, Noe-as-orthodox); science-of-happiness (Kahneman-Diener-Schwarz), insofar as it would render Equiano's case as 'adaptation'

positions.stance: Merleau-Ponty's 'Freedom' chapter — particularly Phenomenology of Perception p.84 (Smith trans., Routledge 1989/1945) and the three-page footnote at 172n1 — retains a Hegelian-Marxist line in which the human situation can abolish the biological one and the social body can 'go limp.'
positions.opposition: Hubert Dreyfus's pragmatic-phenomenological reading of Merleau-Ponty

positions.stance: Pragmatic phenomenology (especially Dreyfus's 'Intelligence without Representation' 2002) loses what Merleau-Ponty's Hegelian strand reveals — namely the resources for political analysis of unequal situations.
positions.opposition: Hubert Dreyfus; Alva Noe (in some respects); the 'background of intentionality' literature insofar as it remains Heideggerian-pragmatic

positions.stance: Security and attachment must be understood in terms of vested interests, which may run at cross-purposes with felt attachment: Equiano can feel attached to the very relationships that subject him.
positions.opposition: Theories that align attachment with practical interest tout court (Noe via Merleau-Ponty as 'common fate')

positions.stance: Afro-Pessimism (Sexton, Wilderson, Moten) correctly diagnoses Equiano's exclusion from systems of intelligibility — 'not ever' admitted — but Gross declines to endorse the program wholesale, retaining instead a rhetorical-humanities methodology that can register the exclusion analytically.
positions.opposition: Strong Afro-Pessimist positions that foreclose the rhetorical-humanities reading; also Sara Ahmed insofar as her social-investment frame presupposes a contract from which Equiano is excluded

positions.stance: Equiano's pathos is not first something he feels nor something observed, but a positing of a social relationship (subjection-as-terror, master-as-gratitude, English-as-identity). 'Was Equiano really happy?' is not directly answerable on Kahneman's instant-utility scale.
positions.opposition: Ed Diener et al.'s positive-emotion functionalism; Kahneman's instant-utility insofar as it presumes state-description; Samuel Johnson's Rambler-60 identification model insofar as it presumes sincere recognition

positions.stance: Equiano's Methodist conversion narrative is not 'rather tiresome' (Wollstonecraft 1789 Analytical Review) but vivifying — the conventional spiritual-autobiography form executes the chapter's analytic claim that Equiano cannot bear himself; only Christ bears.
positions.opposition: Mary Wollstonecraft, Analytical Review 1789, vol. 4, pp. 27-29; secular-rationalist readings of slave-narrative more generally

positions.stance: Alva Noe's claim that perception has a 'rhetorical structure' is the situated-cognition theorist's own admission of the humanities' centrality — a thesis Gross accepts and extends to slavery as 'hostile' environment.
positions.advocate: Daniel M. Gross (taking Noe at his word)
positions.opposition: Reductive cognitivist readings of perception; instant-utility hedonic psychology insofar as it brackets the rhetorical anchoring of well-being reports

tensions.summary: Gross vs. Dreyfus on the right reading of Merleau-Ponty's 'Freedom' chapter. Dreyfus reads Merleau-Ponty pragmatically (background of intentionality, Heideggerian everyday orientation); Gross reads Merleau-Ponty's p.84 and 172n1 as preserving a Hegelian-Marxist strand that pragmatic phenomenology systematically loses, with direct political consequences for analyzing race-based slavery.
tensions.stakes: Whether phenomenology has analytic resources for unequal-political situations or whether it requires supplementation (or replacement) by critical theory.

tensions.summary: Gross vs. Wollstonecraft (Analytical Review 1789) on the literary value of Equiano's Methodist conversion material. Wollstonecraft finds it 'rather tiresome' after the 'blood-turning' first volume; Gross argues it is precisely the conventional spiritual-autobiography form that executes the chapter's analytic — Equiano cannot bear himself, only Christ bears.
tensions.stakes: Whether spiritual-autobiography conventions are formal-religious filler or rhetorical-analytic engines.

tensions.summary: Vested interests vs. felt attachment. Equiano's gratitude to Pascal is sincerely felt (or sincerely performed in retrospect) yet Pascal sells him; Equiano's attachment to Robert King runs alongside King's default on his debt. Carretta's formula is that interests can be vested differently from feelings — and indeed felt attachment may be precisely the vehicle of subjection (Butler 'passionate attachments').
tensions.stakes: Whether 'common fate' attachment models (Noe, orthodox Merleau-Pontian readings) can register the structural asymmetries of master-slave attachment.

tensions.summary: Engaging Afro-Pessimism without endorsing it. The 'not ever' line — Equiano never admitted to systems of intelligibility — runs through the chapter, supported by Sexton, Wilderson, Moten. But Gross's methodological commitment is rhetorical-humanities analysis that registers this exclusion analytically; he stops short of programmatic Afro-Pessimism.
tensions.stakes: Whether rhetorical-situation analysis can do justice to the irreducibility of black social death without dissolving into Afro-Pessimist negation.

tensions.summary: Rhetorical attitude-positing vs. hedonic state-description. 'Was Equiano really happy?' is undecidable on Kahneman's instant-utility scale; Gross's rejoinder is that the question presupposes a state-description model that Equiano's prose itself refuses (layered retrospection, eighteenth-century 'happy = by chance').
tensions.stakes: Whether subjective-well-being measurement can survive the rhetorical analysis it presupposes (per Schwarz-Strack).

tensions.summary: Ahmed's social-investment-promises-return frame (Queer Phenomenology 17) presupposes a contract from which Equiano is excluded. Gross 'amends Ahmed' — Equiano is pressed into service outside the domain of consent or social contract, so the very mechanism Ahmed analyzes is foreclosed.
tensions.stakes: Whether queer phenomenology's tools port over to race-based slavery or require structural revision.
